Consult Summary:
- A 35-year-old male with known hyperthyroidism on thyroxine presents with intermittent frontal headaches, heat intolerance, tachycardia, shortness of breath, unintentional weight loss, reduced appetite, bilateral arm tingling, and decreased libido, occurring mainly during work after changing jobs; clinician plans in-clinic evaluation with cardiovascular and respiratory examination and thyroid function testing to assess thyrotoxicosis and overall symptom cluster.

History:
- Presenting complaint
  - Severe headaches with associated nausea, feeling hot, occasional shortness of breath, tachycardia, reduced appetite, and unintentional weight loss.
  - Tingling in both arms (paresthesias), especially when entering elevators, and decreased libido.
  - Headache episodes are intermittent, mostly at work (in meetings or reading on laptop) and can occur at different times; not clearly migrainous with a consistent pattern.
- Time line
  - Onset approximately after changing jobs; symptoms fluctuate, with episodes at work rather than commute.
- Exacerbating/initiating/relieving factors
  - Initiated or worsened with work stress and prolonged computer use; no clear relief factors described.
- Associated symptoms
  - Nausea during headaches; brief dyspnea at desk; palpitations; possible breathlessness on exertion not reported; no focal neurological deficits described.
- Systems review and negatives
  - Known hyperthyroidism; on thyroxine (dose not documented); adherent.
  - Alcohol: weekly (a couple of glasses); Smokes: none; No recreational drugs reported.
  - No allergies noted.
- Relevant context
  - Occupation: Lawyer in London; high occupational stress (7–8/10).
  - No prior headaches documented before job change; prior medical issues limited to hyperthyroidism.

Past Medical History:
- Hyperthyroidism
  - On thyroxine therapy; adherence reported.
  - Dose, route, and frequency not documented.
- No other medical problems explicitly mentioned.

Medications:
- Thyroxine (dose/route/frequency not documented).

Allergies:
- None reported.

Social History:
- Occupation: Lawyer in London; high workplace stress.
- Alcohol: weekly, a couple of glasses of wine.
- Smoking: no.
- Recreational drugs: no.

Family History:
- Not documented.

Physical Examination:
- No vital signs recorded in transcript.
- No explicit physical examination findings documented.
- Plan: in-clinic evaluation including heart and lung examination.

Investigations:
- Plan to perform blood tests including thyroid function (thyroxine level; TSH, Free T4, Free T3) and other basic labs.
- No imaging results discussed.

Assessment & Plan:
- Issue 1: Suspected thyrotoxicosis / hyperthyroidism in the setting of known hyperthyroidism on thyroxine
  - Plan:
    - In-person clinic evaluation with cardiovascular and respiratory examination.
    - Order thyroid function tests (TSH, Free T4, Free T3) and basic labs; review current thyroxine dose and adherence.
    - Reconcile whether current thyroxine dose may be contributing to symptoms; adjust therapy as indicated after test results.
    - Return to clinic for results assessment and management decisions.
- Issue 2: Headache with nausea (likely migraine/tension-type or secondary to stress)
  - Plan:
    - In-person exam, including assessment of head, neck, and neurological status; overall evaluation of headaches.
    - No imaging or acute interventions described at this time; management to be guided by exam and test results.
- Issue 3: Autonomic symptoms (tachycardia, dyspnea at rest/desk, arm paresthesias) and libido change in context of stress
  - Plan:
    - Evaluate during in-clinic visit; correlate with thyroid status and anxiety/stress response.
    - No specific psychiatric treatment plan documented; plan focuses on in-clinic assessment and thyroid-directed workup.
- Additional plan notes
  - Schedule: Book in-clinic appointment via app; patient notified that his information will be shared with the clinic team to avoid repetition.
  - Follow-up: Contingent on test results and clinical exam; further management decisions to be made after in-person assessment.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx):
- Thyrotoxicosis / Hyperthyroidism (likely due to levothyroxine therapy—over-replacement or high sensitivity)
  - Likelihood: High
  - Rationale: Known hyperthyroidism on thyroxine; symptoms align with thyrotoxic state (tachycardia, heat intolerance, weight loss with reduced appetite, libido changes, intermittent symptoms).
  - Supporting evidence: Tachycardia episodes, weight loss without intentional dieting, heat sensation, decreased libido, adherence to thyroxine.
  - Opposing evidence: No lab confirmation yet; thyroid status not yet quantified.
- Migraine-type or tension-type headache with autonomic symptoms
  - Likelihood: Moderate-High
  - Rationale: Frontal headaches with nausea, work-related triggers, and stress association.
  - Supporting evidence: Headache description, nausea, triggers related to prolonged computer use/work.
  - Opposing evidence: No classic migraine features documented (photophobia/phonophobia/aura) or pattern of progression.
- Anxiety/panic disorder with autonomic symptoms related to work stress
  - Likelihood: Moderate
  - Rationale: High occupational stress with tachycardia, brief dyspnea, and paresthesias; symptom fluctuation.
  - Supporting evidence: Stress level 7–8/10, autonomic symptoms.
  - Opposing evidence: Weight loss and headaches not fully explained by anxiety alone.
- Pheochromocytoma
  - Likelihood: Low
  - Rationale: Headache with tachycardia and weight loss can occur, but rare; additional signs (hypertension, diaphoresis) not described.
  - Supporting evidence: Headache with tachycardia and weight loss.
  - Opposing evidence: No documented hypertension, diaphoresis, or classic triad; overall low pretest probability in this setting.

Quality checks:

  - Vital signs (BP, heart rate, respiratory rate, temperature) not documented.
  - Comprehensive physical examination results missing.
  - Specific thyroid labs and results not yet available.
  - Details of thyroxine dose, route, and frequency not documented.
  - Allergies not explored beyond patient stating none; no explicit “no known drug allergies” statement.
- Conflicts between transcript and DDx
  - No explicit conflicts detected; differential aligns with known history and symptom cluster.
  - “Conflict noted” not required.
- Transcript quality
  - Generally coherent; some minor interruptions/incomplete responses in the dialogue, but the essential clinical content is captured.
  - No inconsistent statements identified beyond lack of objective data (vitals and labs) in the transcript.
